successors.note: The Faucigny passed from France to the House of Savoy under the Treaty of Paris of 1355 (Faucigny page), after this row's end.

capitals.name: Grenoble
capitals.note: Infobox: Grenoble, 'historical capital'. Humbert II's court is placed at Beauvoir-en-Royans on the Humbert II page (undated).

rulers.name: Guigues VII
rulers.note: Dauphin of Viennois, count of Albon, Grenoble, Oisans, Briançon, Embrun and Gap, 1237-1269. Reigned from 1237; the strip starts at the dossier's start (1260). [Reviewer eu-10-g]

rulers.name: John I
rulers.note: Count over several of the same territories, including Embrun but not Gap.

rulers.name: Humbert I (Baron of La Tour du Pin)
rulers.note: Dauphin through his marriage to Anne of Viennois, countess of Albon. The Dauphin of Viennois page lists no dauphin for 1307-1318.

rulers.name: John II
rulers.note: 'Baron of La Tour du Pin, Dauphin of Viennois, ruled 1307-1318' (Dauphin of Viennois page). Added by reviewer eu-10-g to close the 1307-1318 gap.

rulers.name: Humbert II
rulers.note: 'was the Dauphin de Viennois, from 1333 to 1349'; handed his lands and titles to the young French prince Charles on 16 July 1349.

rulers.name: Charles (the future Charles V), first Valois dauphin
rulers.note: The pages give no end year for his rule as dauphin; 1351 is this dossier's end year.

correction.text: The 1260 shape plus the Hautes-Alpes (the counties of Briançon, Embrun and Gap among the titles of Guigues VII), drawn 1260-1267

keyframe_review.note: 9,105 km2: Isère (25 of 31 cells) with a few Drôme, Hautes-Alpes and Savoie cells. No infobox area is given; the Dauphiné page says the province 'roughly corresponded to that of the present-day departments of Isère, Drôme and Hautes-Alpes', and Guigues VII was 'Dauphin of Viennois, Count of Albon, Grenoble, Oisans, Briançon, Embrun and Gap': the Hautes-Alpes (Briançon, Embrun, Gap) are therefore added, since the shape holds 3 of its 22 cells. Right for 1260-1267; the Faucigny joins in 1268. The Drôme cells (5) are kept as drawn, unverified: page budget.

correction.text: The 1260 shape plus the Hautes-Alpes and the Faucigny, inherited by Béatrix (wife of the Dauphin Guigues VII) in 1268

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1268-1271. 'Their daughter, Béatrix, inherited the province in 1268' (Peter II of Savoy having acquired Faucigny by marrying Agnès, the baron's daughter, in 1253); Béatrix married Guigues VII, which placed the lands under the Dauphin de Viennois (Faucigny page; the page does not date the marriage). Faucigny is not in Cliopatria's shape.

correction.text: The 1272 shape plus the Hautes-Alpes (Briançon and Embrun; Gap not listed among John I's territories) and the Faucigny, drawn 1272-1313

keyframe_review.note: 9,291 km2, the 1260 shape with a few more cells (Drôme, Hautes-Alpes, Ardèche), unexplained by the pages. John I (1269-1282) ruled as dauphin and count over several of the same territories, including Embrun but not Gap: the Hautes-Alpes are added whole, the loss of the Gapençais cannot be resolved from the pages and is flagged in notes. Humbert I (1282-1307) 'became, by his marriage, dauphin of Viennois' (Humbert I page, undated marriage): no change of land is dated.

correction.text: The 1314 shape plus the Hautes-Alpes and the Faucigny, drawn 1314-1332

keyframe_review.note: 8,990 km2: the shape loses one Loire cell (300 km2) against 1272; no page explains it (unverified: page budget). The Hautes-Alpes and the Faucigny stay in, as for 1272. Guigues VIII is dauphin 1318-1333 (Dauphin of Viennois page); the page gives no territorial event.

correction.text: The 1333 shape plus the Hautes-Alpes and the Faucigny, drawn 1333-1343

keyframe_review.note: 8,990 km2. 1333: Humbert II takes over the Dauphiné on the death of his brother Guigues VIII, at war with Aymon, Count of Savoy ('they were at war with Aymon, Count of Savoy'); Philip VI arranged a truce within a year. The Hautes-Alpes and the Faucigny stay in.

correction.text: The 1344 shape plus the Hautes-Alpes and the Faucigny, drawn 1344-1351, under Humbert II to 16 July 1349 and then under the French heir Charles

keyframe_review.note: 8,990 km2 to 1351. in 1343 Humbert II decided to sell his domains, titles and rights in the Dauphiné, the 1344 agreement named John, Duke of Normandy as heir, and the Treaty of Romans of 1349 made Charles the successor: on 16 July 1349 Charles became the first Valois dauphin. The Dauphiné stayed 'a distinctive polity, not incorporated into the French kingdom'; Cliopatria draws it to 1351 and the Kingdom of France shape holds Grenoble from 1352, so the shape is kept to 1351.

region.text: Viennois around Grenoble, with the counties of Briançon, Embrun and Gap

ledger.note: 1260: first year of the Cliopatria shape of the Dauphiné of Viennois, centred on Grenoble; the pages give no founding year. Guigues VII is already 'Dauphin of Viennois, Count of Albon, Grenoble, Oisans, Briançon, Embrun and Gap' from 1237 (Dauphin of Viennois page) and the province 'was originally the Dauphiné of Viennois'.

region.text: the Faucigny, inherited by Béatrix, wife of the Dauphin Guigues VII

ledger.note: 1268: the Faucigny comes to the Dauphin's wife. 'Their daughter, Béatrix, inherited the province in 1268', after Peter II of Savoy (who 'acquired Faucigny by marrying Agnès' in 1253); Béatrix married Guigues VII, which placed the lands under the Dauphin de Viennois (marriage undated on the page, so the date of the Dauphin's control is my reading).

16 July 1349: Humbert II hands the Dauphiné to the future Charles V. 'relinquishing his lands and titles on 16 July to the young French prince'; 'Thus in the summer of 1349, the young French prince Charles became the first Dauphin de Viennois' (the Valois line); Faucigny page: 'Faucigny became part of France in 1349'. Same state, same colour (the Dauphiné stays distinct).

region.text: the Dauphiné and the Faucigny as drawn in 1344-1351

ledger.note: 1351: last year of the Cliopatria Dauphiné shape; the Kingdom of France shape holds Grenoble from 1352. The pages give no 1351 event: the sale of 1349 left the Dauphiné 'a distinctive polity, not incorporated into the French kingdom'. A gap-filler should find when the Dauphiné was joined to the kingdom.

wars.name: War of Humbert II with Aymon of Savoy
wars.outcome: Humbert II inherited the Dauphiné in 1333 while at war with Aymon, Count of Savoy; Philip VI arranged a truce within a year. No land changed hands.
wars.note: The page gives no exact date for the truce and names no battle.

wars.name: Savoyard dispute over the Faucigny
wars.outcome: Amadeus VI of Savoy challenged the French purchase, defeated the French in 1354 and obtained the Faucigny under the Treaty of Paris (1355).
wars.note: Fought by the French Dauphin Charles after Humbert II's sale; the years 1352-1355 lie after this row's Cliopatria end.

certainty.note: The frontiers with Savoy, the Provence marquisate and the Rhône bishoprics are feudal and approximate; no treaty line before the Treaty of Paris of 1355.

notes: Cliopatria's Dauphiné shape (about 9,000 km2, Isère plus a few cells) is much smaller than the lands of the Dauphin on the pages: the Dauphin of Viennois page lists the counties of Briançon, Embrun and Gap (the Hautes-Alpes), and the Faucigny (Haute-Savoie) came with Béatrix in 1268 and went to Savoy in 1355. The corrections add the whole Hautes-Alpes and the region 'Faucigny' (not in the gazetteer yet). Not settled: whether Gap was held after 1269 (including Embrun but not Gap for John I); the Drôme cells (the Dauphiné later covered the Drôme, but the Valentinois and Diois are not shown to be the Dauphin's before 1349); the Loire/Ardèche/Savoie stray cells; the 1349-1351 years (the Dauphiné stayed a distinct polity; Cliopatria ends it in 1351, a dissolve at confidence 1); what the Kingdom of France umbrella means for 1260-1349, since Cliopatria lists the Dauphiné as a member of the Kingdom of France while the Humbert II page puts it under the Kingdom of Burgundy (Arles) and the Empire until the sale. The Humbert I page was thin (no territory dates); the 1307-1318 dauphins are not listed on the pages opened. No infobox area on any page opened. Gazetteer names needed: Faucigny. Neighbours with their own dossiers: county-of-savoy (Faucigny loss 1268), capetian-house-of-anjou (Provence), comtat-venaissin, county-of-auvergne.
